1.note: Yahweh is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were a young **child** here and in the next few verses. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Israel was a young nation]

Yahweh is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were his **son**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my people]

2.note: The phrase **They called to them** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. It is unclear who **They** would refer to. The ancient Greek and Syriac translations reflect a reading that has Yahweh calling to the Israelites directly and that includes an initial term that means “the more” or “as much as.” The UST follows this reading. If you prefer to translate according to the Hebrew, there are two possibilities: (1) “They” could refer to the prophets, through whom Yahweh called to the Israelites to repent and obey him. Alternate translation: [The prophets called to them] or [I called to them through the prophets] or (2) it could refer to worshippers of Baal, who called the Israelites away from Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Worshippers of Baal called to them]
The pronoun **they** in this phrase refers to the people of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites went from their faces]

Here the phrase **from their faces** could: (1) represent “from their presence,” referring to the prophets of Yahweh. Or if you chose to divide the words differently as did the ancient Greek and Syriac translators, it would represent “from my presence.” Alternate translation: [from before them] or [from before me] or (2) be a common expression of the culture that means “because of them.” In this case, it could refer to the worshippers of Baal, if that is how you chose to interpret who **They** is in **They called to them** at the beginning of the verse. Alternate translation: [because of them]

The phrase **from their faces** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. You may want to follow an alternative reading from the ancient Greek and Syriac translations, which divided the words differently, reading the pronoun with the verb “they kept sacrificing” (“they” has the same letters as “their”). The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [from my face] or [from me]

3.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I taught** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was he himself who cared for the people of Ephraim. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Yet I myself taught Ephraim to walk]

Yahweh is speaking of his early care for the people of Ephraim as if he as a parent had been teaching a small child and **taught Ephraim to walk**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I cared for Ephraim like a parent teaching a small child to walk]

The phrase **He took them upon his arms** could be translated to mean: (1) that Yahweh picked up Ephraim, pictured as a small child, and carried him in his arms. The UST follows this interpretation. It may be that Hosea is speaking about Yahweh here, or it may be that the original reading continued Yahweh’s speech in the first person, as the ancient Greek and Syriac translations have it. Alternate translation: [I took him up in my arms] or (2) that Yahweh took Ephraim, pictured as a small child, and held onto Ephraim’s arms as Yahweh taught Ephraim to walk. Alternate translation: [He took him by his arms] or [I took him by his arms]

3.q: קָחָ֖⁠ם עַל־זְרֽוֹעֹתָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠לֹ֥א יָדְע֖וּ כִּ֥י רְפָאתִֽי⁠ם
3.note: The plural pronouns **them** and **they** refer to Ephraim as the nation of Israel which is a shift from earlier in this verse where he refers to the nation as the person, **Ephraim**. Throughout this chapter, the pronouns referring to Israel and Ephraim vary between singular and plural. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular here and in the next verses or use the plural throughout as modeled in the UST. Alternate translation: [He took him upon his arms, but he did not know that I healed him]

Yahweh is speaking of caring for the people of Israel as if he **healed them** from sickness. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I cared for them]

4.note: Yahweh is speaking of the kind and gentle ways he led the people of Israel as if they were **cords of humanity** and **bands of love** by which he drew them along. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I led them with gentle kindness and love]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **love**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how I loved them]

4.q: וָ⁠אֶהְיֶ֥ה לָ⁠הֶ֛ם כִּ⁠מְרִ֥ימֵי עֹ֖ל עַ֣ל לְחֵי⁠הֶ֑ם
4.note: The phrase **And I was to them like the lifters of a yoke on their jaws** is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. A yoke is never placed on an animal’s jaws, but on the animal’s neck. Further, if this were an image of release from slavery, it would describe lifting the yoke from the animal, not lifting it on the animal. It seems that the word translated as **yoke** should be pronounced with a different vowel, which would then be the word for “infant.” The word translated as **jaws** also means “cheek.” Therefore, this could mean: (1) Yahweh is continuing the picture of Ephraim as a small child and describing his tender care for them. The UST follows that reading. Alternate translation: [And I was to them like those who lift an infant onto their cheeks] or (2) Yahweh is describing Ephraim as a working animal on which he is lifting a yoke, perhaps as a picture of releasing them from slavery. Alternate translation: [And I was to them like those who lift a yoke on their jaws]

Yahweh is speaking of his care for the people of Israel as if he were a parent who **bent down** and **fed** a small child. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I gently cared for him and fed him]

5.q: לֹ֤א יָשׁוּב֙ אֶל־אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם וְ⁠אַשּׁ֖וּר ה֣וּא מַלְכּ֑⁠וֹ כִּ֥י מֵאֲנ֖וּ לָ⁠שֽׁוּב
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the last phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrases describe. Alternate translation: [Since they refused to return to worship Yahweh, he will not return them to the land of Egypt, but instead, Assyria will be his king]

The pronoun **he** refers to the king of Assyria, while the pronoun **his** refers to Ephraim. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the king of Assyria will be Ephraim‘s king]
The implication is that they refused to return to worshiping Yahweh. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they no longer worship me]

6.note: Yahweh assumes that readers will know the **bars** being referred to are part of the city gates. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and will destroy the bars of his gates]

Yahweh is speaking of the destruction that the sword will cause as if the sword would **devour** its victims like an animal eating its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and will destroy them because of their plans]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and will devour them because of their plans]

The pronoun **their** refers to the Ephraim or the nation of Israel which is a shift from earlier in this verse where he refers to the nation as the person with the pronoun **his**. Throughout this chapter, the pronouns referring to Ephraim and Israel vary between singular and plural. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular here and in the next verses or use the plural throughout as modeled in the UST. Alternate translation: [because of his plans]

7.note: Yahweh is speaking of his people abandoning their loyalty to him as if they were physically **turning away from** him to walk in a different direction. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are determined to abandon me]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **him** and **he**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Though they call to me on high, I will not raise them up at all]

8.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express the anguish and reluctance he feels at the thought of giving up his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will not give you up, Ephraim or surrender you, Israel!]

Yahweh is using the question form to express how unwilling he is to destroy his people as he destroyed Admah. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I will not make you like Admah or set you like Zeboiim!]

The point of this comparison is that while the cities of **Admah** and **Zeboiim** were completely destroyed (see Deuteronomy 29:23), this is something that Yahweh does not want to do to the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [How can I completely destroy you like Admah and Zebeoiim]

Yahweh is speaking of the turmoil of his strong feelings of anguish as if his **heart** were physically **turned over within** him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My heart is overwhelmed within me]

The expression **is turned over** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [This situation makes my heart turn over within me]

Here Yahweh speaks of his **heart** as it represents where his feelings and desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My inner being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassions**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my feelings of compassion for you]

The expression **are aroused** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [rise up]

9.note: Yahweh is using **the burning of my nose** as a common expression of the culture to mean “my fierce anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my fierce anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [angrily]

10.note: This could be: (1) Hosea speaking about Yahweh as in the UST or (2) Yahweh speaking of himself in the third person. Alternate translation: [They will come after me, Yahweh]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a lion** roars loudly and powerfully, so Yahweh will summon his people with a loud, powerful voice. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he will roar powerfully to summon his people]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he roars** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is he himself who roars. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [When he himself roars]

Yahweh is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were his **sons** returning to their father. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who belong to him]

11.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a bird** would be timid, fearful, and trembling in response to a lion’s roar, so the people of Israel will hurry back from exile with respectful fear when Yahweh summons them to return. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They will return with fear and trembling from Egypt]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a dove** is gentle and docile, so the people of Israel will come back without objections from the land of Assyria, ready to obey Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and other returns from Assyria like a dove that docilely returns home]

Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person in the phrase **the declaration of Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [it is I, Yahweh, who is declaring this]

12.note: Yahweh is speaking of the constant lying of the people of Ephraim as if they had **surrounded me with lies** on every side. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has completely deceived me with lies]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **deceit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the house of Israel is constantly trying to deceive me]

Yahweh is using **roams with God** as a common expression of the culture to mean “remains loyal to God.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [remains loyal to God]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]

12.q: וִֽ⁠יהוּדָ֗ה עֹ֥ד רָד֙ עִם־אֵ֔ל וְ⁠עִם־קְדוֹשִׁ֖ים נֶאֱמָֽן
12.note: The sentence **But Judah still roams with God, and is established with the Holy One** could mean: (1) that although Israel is far from God, Judah is still following him. The ULT and UST follow that reading, or (2) that the word translated as “God” refers to the false god Baal, and the word translated as “the Holy One” refers to the lesser gods who serve Baal. This could be possible because the word is plural, but words for God are often plural to indicate his majesty. Alternate translation: [But Judah still roams with a god, and is established with the holy ones]

The expression **is established** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the Holy One establishes them]
